Best AI Tools for Data Analysts: Querying, Cleaning and Insight Generation

Data analysts can use AI to accelerate cleaning, summarization, and query support while keeping validation and interpretation in human hands.

By LokkeeVerse · 21 min read

Best AI Tools for Data Analysts: Querying, Cleaning and Insight Generation

Data analysts play an important role in helping businesses understand performance, identify problems, and make better decisions. However, turning raw data into useful insights can involve hours of writing SQL queries, cleaning spreadsheets, correcting inconsistent values, creating charts, and preparing reports for stakeholders.

Artificial intelligence is making many of these tasks faster. Modern AI tools can help analysts generate SQL, write Python scripts, identify data quality issues, explore datasets, create visualizations, and explain analytical findings in plain language.

The biggest advantage is not simply producing results faster. It is reducing repetitive work so analysts can spend more time asking meaningful questions, validating findings, and explaining what the data means for a business.

This guide explores the best AI tools for data analysts, including solutions for querying, data cleaning, visualization, reporting, and insight generation.

What Are AI Tools for Data Analysts?

AI tools for data analysts are applications that use artificial intelligence to support the process of collecting, preparing, exploring, interpreting, and communicating data.

Depending on the tool, analysts can use AI to:

  • Generate SQL queries from natural-language questions.
  • Write Python scripts for data analysis.
  • Identify missing values, duplicates, and inconsistent formats.
  • Suggest data cleaning and transformation steps.
  • Explore datasets and identify potential patterns.
  • Generate charts, dashboards, and summaries.
  • Explain statistical findings in accessible language.
  • Automate parts of recurring reporting workflows.
  • Document analytical processes and query logic.
  • Prepare reports and recommendations for decision-makers.

Some tools work directly with spreadsheets, while others connect to databases, analytical notebooks, or business intelligence platforms. Choosing the right tool depends on where your data lives, how much technical control you need, and whether your analysis must be reproducible.

Best AI Tools for Data Analysts

1. ChatGPT — Best for Exploratory Data Analysis and Insight Generation

ChatGPT is a flexible AI assistant that can help analysts understand datasets, write code, investigate patterns, and communicate findings. Depending on the available features and plan, it can also analyze uploaded files and use computational tools to support data exploration.

It is useful when an analyst needs to investigate an unfamiliar dataset or answer questions before building a permanent dashboard.

Key uses include:

  • Analyzing supported CSV and Excel files.
  • Generating Python code for data manipulation.
  • Explaining statistical concepts and results.
  • Identifying possible outliers and unusual patterns.
  • Creating charts and visualizations.
  • Drafting summaries and analytical reports.
  • Writing and explaining SQL queries.

For example, an analyst could upload a sales dataset and ask which products generated the most revenue, which months performed best, and whether any regions experienced a decline in sales.

ChatGPT can help explore those questions, but the analyst should verify the calculations, investigate unusual findings, and distinguish correlation from causation. Its output should be treated as a starting point rather than unquestionable evidence.

Best for: exploratory analysis, data interpretation, coding assistance, and report preparation.

2. Microsoft Copilot in Excel — Best for Spreadsheet Analysis and Cleaning

Microsoft Copilot can assist with spreadsheet tasks within supported Microsoft Excel experiences. It is useful for analysts who spend much of their time working with business reports, sales records, budgets, operational data, and other tabular information.

Instead of manually searching for every formula or transformation, users can describe the task they want to perform and use AI assistance to develop an approach.

Key uses include:

  • Helping write or explain spreadsheet formulas.
  • Exploring trends in tabular data.
  • Supporting data organization and transformation.
  • Generating summaries and visualizations.
  • Assisting with calculations and reporting.
  • Helping interpret patterns in spreadsheet data.

For example, an analyst could ask for help identifying unusual changes in monthly revenue, calculating growth rates, or creating a summary of sales by region.

AI suggestions still require validation. Check formula references, date handling, missing values, and aggregation logic before relying on the output.

Copilot availability depends on the Microsoft 365 environment, subscription, and organizational settings. Confirm that your version of Excel supports the features you intend to use.

Best for: spreadsheet-heavy workflows and organizations already using Microsoft Excel.

3. Claude — Best for Complex Analysis and Analytical Reporting

Claude can help analysts reason through complex questions, work with substantial amounts of supporting documentation, develop code, and turn findings into clear written explanations.

It is particularly useful when the analysis involves multiple assumptions, business rules, data dictionaries, or source documents that need to be considered together.

Key uses include:

  • Writing and explaining SQL queries.
  • Developing Python analysis scripts.
  • Reviewing analytical methodology.
  • Summarizing extensive research and documentation.
  • Drafting reports for business stakeholders.
  • Explaining findings and their limitations.
  • Helping structure complex analytical investigations.

For example, an analyst investigating customer churn might provide a data dictionary, a summary of the available variables, and preliminary results. Claude can help organize possible explanations, suggest additional analyses, and draft a report that distinguishes observed patterns from hypotheses.

As with any AI assistant, numerical outputs and technical suggestions need independent verification. Make sure that the analysis uses the correct population, definitions, and time period.

Best for: complex analytical reasoning, long-form reporting, and working with extensive context.

4. Julius AI — Best for Asking Questions About Data in Plain English

Julius AI is designed to help users analyze datasets through a conversational interface. It can be useful for analysts who want to explore a spreadsheet or dataset without manually writing every calculation or visualization from scratch.

Instead of beginning with a notebook, a user can ask questions about the available data and iterate on the analysis.

Key uses include:

  • Exploring uploaded datasets.
  • Asking questions in natural language.
  • Generating charts and summaries.
  • Supporting exploratory statistical analysis.
  • Helping identify trends and potential anomalies.
  • Iterating on analytical questions through conversation.

For example, a small-business analyst could examine transaction records and ask which product categories contribute the most revenue, whether average order value changes over time, and which regions warrant further investigation.

The results depend on the quality of the data and the tool's ability to interpret the question correctly. Check the underlying calculations and inspect the code or methodology when available.

Review supported file sizes, database connections, export options, and current subscription limits before using Julius AI for a regular business workflow.

Best for: conversational data exploration and analysts who want a low-friction starting point.

5. Google Gemini — Best for Google Workspace and Data Science Assistance

Google Gemini can support analytical work through code generation, data interpretation, and integrations with supported Google products. Its usefulness depends on whether you are working with spreadsheets, notebooks, cloud data platforms, or general analytical questions.

Analysts who use Google Sheets, BigQuery, or Google Colab may find relevant Gemini-powered capabilities within those environments.

Key uses include:

  • Helping generate spreadsheet formulas.
  • Explaining SQL and Python code.
  • Supporting data exploration and analysis.
  • Summarizing analytical documentation.
  • Assisting with notebook-based workflows.
  • Supporting work within compatible Google data tools.

For example, an analyst using BigQuery might use an appropriate AI assistant to draft a query for monthly revenue by customer segment, then review and run the query against the intended tables.

The general Gemini assistant and specialized features in Google data products are not interchangeable. Confirm the available integrations, permissions, and capabilities for your particular environment.

Best for: analysts who work extensively with Google Workspace, BigQuery, or Colab.

6. GitHub Copilot — Best for SQL and Python Coding Assistance

GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant that can help data analysts write, explain, and improve code in supported development environments.

It is especially useful for analysts who use SQL, Python, R, or notebooks to prepare data and perform repeatable analysis.

Key uses include:

  • Generating SQL query drafts.
  • Writing Python data-cleaning functions.
  • Explaining unfamiliar code.
  • Creating reusable transformation logic.
  • Helping write tests for data processing.
  • Documenting analytical scripts.
  • Assisting with debugging.

For example, a Python analyst could ask Copilot for help writing a function that standardizes date formats, handles missing values, and validates required columns before a dataset is processed.

The generated code should be reviewed for correctness, performance, and edge cases. A cleaning function that works on one example may fail when it encounters unexpected formats or a different data type.

Best for: technical analysts who regularly write and maintain SQL or Python code.

7. Hex — Best for Collaborative SQL and Python Analysis

Hex is a collaborative data workspace that supports analytical workflows involving SQL, Python, notebooks, and visualizations. Its AI-assisted features can help analysts explore data, develop queries, and work through analytical tasks in a shared environment.

It is particularly relevant to teams that need to move from an initial question to a reproducible investigation that colleagues can inspect.

Key uses include:

  • Developing and running SQL queries.
  • Performing Python-based analysis.
  • Exploring warehouse data.
  • Creating visualizations and analytical notebooks.
  • Sharing work with teammates.
  • Documenting and iterating on analysis.

For example, a product analytics team could investigate declining user engagement by querying event data, calculating retention metrics, and presenting the findings in a shared notebook.

Hex is more specialized than a general-purpose chatbot. It is worth considering when your work involves ongoing analytical projects, connected data sources, and collaboration rather than occasional spreadsheet questions.

Best for: analytics teams working with SQL, Python, and shared analytical notebooks.

8. Power BI Copilot — Best for Business Intelligence and Reporting

Microsoft Power BI is a business intelligence platform used to model data, build dashboards, and distribute reports. Its Copilot capabilities can assist with supported analytical and reporting tasks, depending on the workspace, licensing, and configuration.

For analysts, the value lies in combining AI assistance with the broader process of turning business data into reusable reports.

Key uses include:

  • Helping explore data models.
  • Assisting with report creation.
  • Supporting summaries of analytical findings.
  • Helping users interact with supported reports using natural language.
  • Supporting the development of business intelligence content.

For example, an analyst might create a sales dashboard containing revenue, order volume, regional performance, and product trends, then use available AI features to help summarize important changes for management.

Power BI requires careful data modeling. Incorrect relationships, ambiguous metric definitions, and poorly designed measures can produce misleading results even when the visualizations look professional.

Copilot features may require particular licensing or Microsoft Fabric capacity. Confirm current requirements before planning a deployment.

Best for: business analysts, reporting teams, and organizations using Microsoft's analytics ecosystem.

9. Tableau — Best for Data Visualization and Interactive Dashboards

Tableau is a business intelligence platform designed to help users explore and communicate data through interactive visualizations. Its AI-related features can assist with aspects of analytical exploration, reporting, and insight delivery, depending on the product and subscription.

It is particularly useful when stakeholders need to explore data themselves rather than receive only static reports.

Key uses include:

  • Building interactive dashboards.
  • Exploring relationships between variables.
  • Communicating trends through visualizations.
  • Supporting analytical storytelling.
  • Helping deliver insights to business users.
  • Using available AI features to support analytical workflows.

For example, a retail analyst could create a dashboard that allows managers to explore sales by product category, region, and period, making it easier to investigate changes in performance.

A dashboard should do more than display attractive charts. Select visualizations that answer specific questions, label metrics clearly, and avoid implying causation when the data only demonstrates an association.

Best for: analysts who need interactive visual reporting and stakeholder-facing dashboards.

10. Snowflake Cortex Analyst — Best for Natural-Language Questions About Warehouse Data

Snowflake Cortex Analyst is designed to help users query structured data in Snowflake through natural-language questions, using the supported semantic and data configuration.

This is particularly relevant to organizations that store business data in Snowflake and want to make it easier for users to investigate approved datasets.

Key uses include:

  • Translating business questions into analytical queries.
  • Exploring structured warehouse data.
  • Supporting conversational analytics.
  • Working with defined business metrics and data relationships.
  • Helping business users investigate data without writing every query manually.

For example, a sales manager might ask for revenue by region over the last quarter, while the underlying system uses configured definitions to map the question to the appropriate data.

Natural-language querying is only as reliable as the data definitions, permissions, and semantic context behind it. Validate generated SQL, control access to sensitive data, and test common questions before rolling the system out broadly.

Best for: organizations that use Snowflake and want controlled, natural-language access to warehouse data.

11. Databricks Genie — Best for Conversational Analytics on Databricks Data

Databricks Genie is designed to let users ask questions about data using natural language within a configured Databricks environment. It can help organizations make structured data more accessible to business users while keeping analysis connected to the underlying data platform.

Key uses include:

  • Asking questions about supported datasets in plain language.
  • Supporting conversational analytics.
  • Helping users investigate business metrics.
  • Exploring data through configured analytical contexts.
  • Reducing the need for users to write every query manually.

For example, a logistics analyst could investigate delivery performance by region, compare average delivery times, and explore whether delays are concentrated in specific periods.

A reliable deployment requires clear metric definitions, appropriate permissions, tested questions, and oversight of the generated results. Natural-language responses should not replace established reporting controls.

Best for: data teams and organizations already working with Databricks.

12. OpenRefine — Best for Structured Data Cleaning

OpenRefine is an open-source tool designed for working with messy tabular data. It is particularly useful for cleaning and transforming datasets through repeatable operations.

Although it is not primarily a general-purpose AI chatbot, it deserves a place in a data analyst's toolkit because data quality is foundational to reliable analysis. AI assistance can complement structured cleaning workflows when appropriate.

Key uses include:

  • Standardizing inconsistent text values.
  • Identifying duplicate or near-duplicate records.
  • Cleaning inconsistent categories.
  • Transforming columns.
  • Reviewing data patterns.
  • Keeping track of cleaning operations.

Imagine a dataset where the same city appears as "Lagos," "lagos," and "LAGOS." OpenRefine can help identify and standardize these values so they are grouped correctly in reports.

Cleaning rules should be reviewed carefully. Similar-looking names may refer to different entities, and automatically merging records can introduce errors.

Best for: analysts working with inconsistent CSV, spreadsheet, and other tabular datasets.

Best AI Tools by Data Analysis Task

Different stages of analysis require different capabilities. The most useful tool for writing a query may not be the best one for cleaning records or publishing a management dashboard.

Best AI Tools for SQL Querying

SQL is central to many analytical workflows because it allows analysts to retrieve, join, filter, aggregate, and transform structured data.

Useful options include:

  • GitHub Copilot for drafting and explaining SQL.
  • ChatGPT for query design and troubleshooting.
  • Claude for working through complex query logic.
  • Hex for collaborative SQL analysis.
  • Snowflake Cortex Analyst for supported natural-language querying in Snowflake.
  • Databricks Genie for conversational analytics in Databricks.

When generating a query, provide the database type, table names, column definitions, join relationships, and intended metric. Review the generated query before execution, particularly when it accesses large tables or changes data.

Best AI Tools for Data Cleaning

Data cleaning includes handling missing values, standardizing categories, correcting formats, detecting duplicates, and validating records.

Useful options include:

  • Microsoft Copilot in Excel for supported spreadsheet tasks.
  • ChatGPT for generating cleaning code and investigating anomalies.
  • GitHub Copilot for reusable Python functions.
  • OpenRefine for structured transformations.
  • Google Gemini for supported spreadsheet and notebook workflows.

Always retain the original dataset and document significant transformations. Check how each cleaning rule affects record counts and key metrics before moving to analysis.

Best AI Tools for Visualization

Visualizations help analysts communicate findings and explore patterns that may be difficult to identify in raw tables.

Useful options include:

  • Power BI for business intelligence dashboards.
  • Tableau for interactive visual analytics.
  • ChatGPT for exploratory chart generation.
  • Julius AI for conversational chart creation.
  • Hex for notebook-based visualization.

Choose the chart based on the analytical question. Line charts are often useful for changes over time, bar charts for category comparisons, and scatter plots for exploring relationships between numerical variables.

Avoid choosing a chart simply because it looks impressive.

Best AI Tools for Insight Generation and Reporting

Insight generation involves interpreting the results, determining what they mean, and explaining the implications for a business or organization.

Useful options include:

  • ChatGPT for exploratory analysis and summaries.
  • Claude for analytical narratives and report drafts.
  • Julius AI for conversational exploration.
  • Power BI for distributing business intelligence reports.
  • Tableau for communicating interactive findings.

A useful report should explain what changed, how large the change was, which groups were affected, what evidence supports the conclusion, and what further investigation may be needed.

Avoid presenting AI-generated explanations as proven causes unless the analysis supports that conclusion.

How to Choose the Right AI Tool for Your Workflow

Start with Where Your Data Lives

If most of your work happens in Excel, begin by evaluating spreadsheet-integrated assistance. If your organization uses a cloud data warehouse, consider tools that can work within that environment.

For occasional CSV analysis, a general-purpose assistant may be enough. For recurring reports or large datasets, an integrated analytics platform may be more appropriate.

Decide How Much Technical Control You Need

Some tools emphasize conversational analysis and automatic visualizations. Others let you inspect SQL, Python, transformations, and notebook cells.

If your work requires reproducibility, auditing, or complex statistical methods, prefer workflows where you can review and rerun the underlying calculations.

Consider the Scale of Your Work

A small spreadsheet and a warehouse containing billions of records are different problems. Check supported data sizes, query execution costs, refresh requirements, and integration limits before adopting a tool for large-scale analysis.

Evaluate Privacy and Permissions

Analytical datasets may contain customer details, employee records, financial information, or other sensitive data.

Review data-handling policies, access controls, retention terms, and organizational requirements before uploading files or connecting an AI assistant to a database. Use read-only access where appropriate and avoid placing credentials or confidential information into prompts.

Check Costs and Existing Integrations

A tool may look affordable in isolation but become expensive when you add usage fees, workspace requirements, data warehouse compute, or premium licenses.

Evaluate whether the tool works with your existing spreadsheet, database, notebook, and reporting environment before purchasing a new platform.

A Practical AI Workflow for Data Analysts

AI can help throughout an analysis project, but reliable results still require a clear sequence of steps.

Step 1: Define the Business Question

Start by identifying the decision or problem the analysis should address.

For example, rather than asking "Analyze sales," define a more specific question: "Why did revenue decline in the previous quarter, and which product categories contributed most to the decline?"

A focused question helps determine which data is required and which metrics matter.

Step 2: Inspect and Clean the Data

Check the available columns, data types, missing values, duplicates, and date ranges. Use a suitable tool to suggest cleaning rules, but verify each transformation.

Keep a copy of the original data so you can compare results and recover from mistakes.

Step 3: Query the Relevant Records

Use SQL or another appropriate method to extract the data needed for the question. AI can help draft the query, but you should confirm that the joins, filters, and aggregation logic match the business definitions.

Run small validation checks before executing expensive queries against large datasets.

Step 4: Explore the Data

Calculate relevant metrics, compare groups, investigate outliers, and examine changes over time.

Use Python, a notebook, a spreadsheet, or a conversational analysis tool depending on the complexity of the investigation.

Avoid stopping at the first interesting pattern. Test alternative explanations and examine whether the result is robust.

Step 5: Create Visualizations

Choose charts that make the important comparisons clear. Label axes, identify the time period, and explain any unusual metric definitions.

Use a dashboard when stakeholders need to explore multiple dimensions, and a focused chart when one comparison communicates the result more clearly.

Step 6: Interpret and Communicate Findings

Use an AI assistant to help organize the report, explain technical results in plain language, and identify questions that remain unanswered.

Separate confirmed findings from hypotheses. State limitations and recommend follow-up analyses when the available evidence is incomplete.

Step 7: Validate and Document the Result

Recalculate important metrics independently, review generated SQL or Python, and document the data source, filters, assumptions, and transformations.

For recurring analysis, convert successful steps into reusable queries, scripts, or documented workflows instead of relying on an undocumented conversation.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Using AI for Data Analysis

  • Trusting a generated number without checking the calculation.
  • Ignoring missing values, duplicates, or inconsistent categories.
  • Using SQL joins that accidentally duplicate records.
  • Treating correlation as proof of causation.
  • Allowing an AI assistant to access sensitive data without proper controls.
  • Generating dashboards without clear metric definitions.
  • Applying automated cleaning rules without checking their effects.
  • Running expensive queries without reviewing the generated SQL.
  • Reporting AI-generated explanations as established facts.
  • Failing to document the analytical process so others can reproduce the result.

The strongest analysts use AI to accelerate investigation while maintaining control over data quality, calculations, and conclusions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best AI tool for data analysts?

There is no single best tool for every workflow. ChatGPT is useful for exploratory analysis, Microsoft Copilot in Excel supports spreadsheet work, GitHub Copilot helps with SQL and Python coding, Julius AI offers conversational data exploration, and Power BI or Tableau supports business intelligence reporting.

Choose based on your data sources, technical requirements, and the type of output you need.

Can AI write SQL queries for data analysts?

Yes. AI coding assistants and data platforms can generate SQL from written instructions. However, analysts must verify the table relationships, filters, aggregation logic, permissions, and database dialect before using a query.

Can AI clean a dataset automatically?

AI can suggest transformations, identify inconsistent values, generate cleaning code, and help standardize records. However, automated cleaning can make incorrect assumptions. Review the changes, preserve the original data, and validate record counts and important metrics afterward.

Can AI analyze Excel files?

Yes. Depending on the tool and available features, analysts can use ChatGPT, Claude, Julius AI, or spreadsheet-integrated assistants to investigate supported Excel files, calculate metrics, generate summaries, and create charts.

File-size limits, supported formats, and available features vary by provider.

Can AI replace data analysts?

AI can automate portions of querying, cleaning, visualization, and reporting, but effective analysis requires more than generating outputs. Analysts must define the right questions, understand business context, validate results, investigate uncertainty, and communicate recommendations.

AI is best treated as a productivity tool that supports analytical judgment.

Are free AI tools enough to learn data analysis?

Free access can be enough to begin learning SQL, Python, spreadsheets, visualization, and basic analytical reasoning. A beginner can start with sample datasets, a spreadsheet application, a programming notebook, and an AI assistant for explanations.

Paid tools may become useful when you need larger data limits, advanced integrations, collaboration, or recurring business workflows.

Is AI-generated data analysis reliable?

AI can produce useful results, but it can also misinterpret a dataset, generate incorrect code, or present an unsupported explanation confidently. Verify important calculations, inspect the underlying code or queries, and validate findings against the original data.

Final Thoughts

AI is making data analysis more accessible by helping analysts query information, clean messy datasets, explore patterns, and communicate results more efficiently. The most useful tool depends on whether you spend your time in spreadsheets, SQL editors, Python notebooks, or business intelligence platforms.

For a practical starting setup, use ChatGPT for exploratory analysis and explanations, Microsoft Copilot in Excel if spreadsheet work dominates your day, and GitHub Copilot if you regularly write SQL or Python. Add Power BI or Tableau when you need reusable dashboards, or consider a platform such as Hex when collaborative notebook-based analysis is central to your work.

Start with one repetitive task, compare the AI-assisted result with a verified manual result, and document a workflow you can repeat. The goal is not merely to produce more charts or queries. It is to turn reliable data into insights that help people make better decisions.
